text.en:
On a dark night in the village, Pavan saw thousands of stars. His grandfather pointed to seven bright stars shaped like a big spoon.
"That is Saptarshi," he said. "Follow its edge and you will find the Pole Star."

Stars are huge balls of hot glowing gas that make their own light. The Sun is our nearest star. Other stars look small because they are very far away.
Groups of stars that seem to form a pattern are called constellations. Examples are Saptarshi (the Great Bear or Big Dipper) and Orion.
The Pole Star stays almost in the same place in the northern sky because it is above the North Pole. Travellers used it to find north. All other stars seem to move across the sky as the Earth turns.
Stars are giant balls of hot gas that make their own light. The Sun is a star.
Other stars look tiny because they are very far away.
A group of stars forming a pattern is a constellation, like Saptarshi.
The Pole Star shows north and stays almost fixed in the sky.

problem.en: Why does the Sun look so much bigger than the other stars?

text.en: The Sun is a star like the others.

why.en: It is not special in kind.

text.en: But it is much closer to us.

why.en: Distance changes how big it looks.

text.en: Other stars are so far away they look like tiny dots.

why.en: Nearness makes the Sun look large.

prompt.en: A friend says stars twinkle because they are small lamps. How will you explain?

requiredIdeas.en: Stars are huge hot balls of gas, not lamps.
They look small because they are very far away.

points.en: Stars make their own light; the Sun is a star.
A constellation is a pattern of stars.
